entries.missing: ^ inside a compiled body, where the same ^ builds (xor ...) at the term door
entries.detail: OPERATOR_LOWERINGS maps __xor__ to the symbol xor, so S-term a ^ b is (xor a b); the same operator inside @m.define raises 'the operator BitXor has no MeTTa function. MeTTa has no bitwise operators'. The twin reaches xor as a free name instead, bound with m.fn so the Python stays valid. & and | diverge the same way and are the reason math_exp_random's equation lowers differently from its original.

entries.missing: MeTTa's (and ...) inside a compiled body
entries.detail: Python's `and` in a compiled body is Python's `and`: it lowers to (let* ((v A)) (if (py-truthy v) B v)), short-circuiting on truthiness. The original writes (and (<= $lo $x) (<= $x $hi)), MeTTa's own generate-and-test over two values. The operator that would mean it, &, is refused in a body. So the equation stored is not the equation the example stores, and the twin's extra inferences are that lowering.

entries.missing: a compiled body naming a hyphenated function it did not define
entries.detail: A body resolves a free name EXACTLY (the fallback from sqrt_math to sqrt-math was removed on purpose), and a body may name ITSELF in either spelling. So fib-tr compiles, and fib calling fib-tr does not: 'fib_tr is not a parameter of fib, not a function the engine knows'. The twin writes fib's equation at the container door instead, m += S["="](S.fib(V.n), S["fib-tr"](V.n, 0, 1)).

entries.missing: a lowercase symbol as data inside a compiled body
entries.detail: (= (spin $n) (if (> $n 0) (spin (- $n 1)) done)) answers the SYMBOL done. In a compiled body a capitalised free name becomes a constructor and a lowercase one is resolved as a function, so `done` raises and `Done` would store the wrong atom. The twin writes spin at the container door. There is no attribute form either: S.done inside a body is an ast.Attribute, which the compiled subset has no case for.

entries.missing: a module name that resolves without an importing file
entries.detail: import! has no dedicated Python door, which the term builder covers: m.eval(S["import!"](S["&self"], S.fibsmart)) is a legal zero-string spelling. What it cannot do is RESOLVE: a bare module name resolves relative to the importing FILE, and a Python-authored program has no file, so the engine answers `source_sink fibsmart does not exist`. The twin names the path, S["examples/basics/fibsmart"].

entries.missing: two stacked @m.define clauses of one name that fix no literal head, which raise IndexError instead of stacking or refusing
entries.section: correction to §9c's definitional decorator: its two shapes are not interchangeable, and the function shape CRASHES where it owes a refusal
entries.detail: DEFECT, not a missing spelling, found writing this twin and reproduced in three files. Minimal case: `@m.define(name='oc')\ndef oc1(a): return a` followed by `@m.define(name='oc')\ndef oc3(a, b, c): return a + (b + c)` raises `IndexError: list assignment index out of range` at _define_twins.replace_twin_clause. Root cause: _space_definitions._locate_clause answers a replacement index whenever an earlier clause has the SAME patterns (both `{}` here, since neither fixes a literal), and _store_clause then calls replace_twin_clause(dispatcher, that_index, ...) on `twin_dispatcher(fn)`, which is keyed by the PYTHON function name (`oc3`) and is therefore a fresh dispatcher with no clauses. Arity is not consulted, so two clauses of DIFFERENT arity under one name hit it as well. Two consequences: the crash, and the design underneath it, that a second patternless clause is located as a REDEFINITION of the first rather than an alternative beside it, which is P14.3's own note that stacked @define clauses cannot express non-exclusive equations on one head. curry (`overloaded-curry`, two arities), multicall (`mycalc`, two alternatives) and functionremoval/functionremovalspec (`f`, two alternatives) all take the @rules shape because of it. The fix is either to key the twin dispatcher by the METTA name so the clause list and the dispatcher agree, or to refuse the second clause with the sentence _validate_clause_order already writes for the other collisions.

entries.missing: a compiled body that stores the equation the example stores, rather than one that only answers alike
entries.section: correction to what the twins lane proves
entries.detail: The lane compares ANSWERS up to alpha-equivalence and the SET OF HEADS a (= $head $body) match answers; it never compares the bodies, so a compiled body that lowers to a different equation than the example writes passes silently. Measured 2026-08-22 by dumping (= $h $b) from both sides in fresh processes and matching under alpha-equivalence (ai-tmp/equation_diff.py on the p14-twins-f worktree): SEVEN of the 69 examples in basics/, control/ and types/ store different equations, and only one of them, math_exp_random, had said so. Four lowerings account for all seven. (1) `==` and `!=` in a compiled body are `(py-eq a b)` and `(not (py-eq a b))`, the prelude's Python equality, where the originals write `(== a b)`: basics/factorial, basics/fibsmart, basics/xor and control/tests program3. The operator table calls `==` taken for exactly this reason and the method form `a.eq(b)` builds `(== a b)` at the TERM door, so what is missing is a body spelling, not a design decision. (2) A condition whose syntax is not boolean-valued wraps in `(py-truthy ...)`: basics/xor. (3) An assignment is a one-pair `let*` where the original writes `let`: control/eval and control/tests program1. (4) A generator body is a superposition of its yielded answers, so a single yielded form is wrapped in a ONE-element `(superpose (...))`: control/metta4_streams. That last one is a free elision, since a superposition over one alternative IS that alternative; the non-generator body `return superpose(k, counter(k + 1, n)) if k < n else empty()` stores the original's equation to the atom, and was measured doing so. All seven twins now say which of these they carry. The lane could catch the class by comparing stored bodies under alpha-equivalence as well as heads, which is what the measurement above does in forty lines. [measured: seven of 69 examples store equations that differ under alpha-equivalence; command=ai-tmp/equation_diff.py; fixture=the basics, control and types twins against their .metta originals in fresh processes; commit=ddaa528d0cc463d42efa5f86eb194fad77f860f8]

entries.section: §9f input tuples against output Answers (the pipe: kb += (t for t in source()))

entries.detail: `foldall` enumerates its generator itself, so the generator has to reach it as a TERM and the space has to sit inside that term. entries.missing: functools.reduce in a compiled body, where sum() already lowers to foldl-atom
entries.detail: Three of this file's four higher-order forms are already Python syntax in the compiled subset, measured 2026-08-22: `[x + 1 for x in (1, 2, 3)]` compiles to `(map-atom (1 2 3) (|-> ($x) (+ $x 1)))`, adding an `if` compiles to a `filter-atom` inside it, and `sum((1, 2, 3, 4))` compiles to `(foldl-atom (1 2 3 4) 0 +)`.
